Kingrinder P2 Manual Coffee Grinder

Super budget-friendly brew grinder with top-notch burrs and big flavor clarity, if you can handle the static.

IntroductionP2 Grinder

Kingrinder quietly entered the crowded manual grinder scene without the fanfare of brands like Timemore or 1Zpresso. But that doesn’t mean they tiptoe. The P-series, made up of the P0 ($25), P1 ($35), and our main event today, the P2 ($44), drops into the budget coffee world with some serious noise. We’re talking sub‑$50 pricing, real stainless steel burrs, and adjustment ranges that sound like they belong on gear twice the price.

The P2, the most advanced in the P-series, features a heptagonal burr (7 point, with “point” referring to the number of cutting edges or vanes on the burr) meant to enhance grind consistency and minimize fines. While the specs suggest a 33-micron change per click, our testing revealed a much finer effective resolution of about 15µm, putting it firmly in espresso territory on paper. We will explore how that translates to the cup later in the review. Unlike the P1 (six point burrs) and the P0 (five point burrs with a really aggressive “grab” area), the P2 delivers a cup profile that’s notably bright and on the edge of “clean”, particularly for pour‑over and drip lovers.

While Kingrinder’s name might not carry the same cachet as Kino or 1Zpresso, the company’s grinders are becoming folk heroes in the forums. It’s marketed mostly by spec‑chasing online sellers and subreddit snackers, while community reviews praise the P2’s tuning range and portability but note limits in ergonomics and longevity.

What often gets overlooked, though, is that Kingrinder also makes a premium K‑series lineup – including the flagship K6 – that competes with the big players using full‑metal bodies, larger burrs, and external adjustments. The P2 borrows DNA from the lower end K lineup, sporting a seven‑point stainless steel burr similar to what’s found in the K1, but paired up with a budget grind adjustment system, and wrapped in a stripped‑down plastic body for travel‑friendly weight and cost savings.

At 330 grams, the P2 is shockingly light. That featherweight status makes it a backpack favorite for campers, students, and AeroPress nerds (though spoiler alert: it doesn’t fit inside the AeroPress chamber). And when you compare it to something like the 1Zpresso Q-Air — which we just reviewed on CoffeeGeek — the contrast in build and experience becomes evident. The Q-Air feels a bit more like an instrument. The P2? A surprisingly capable toy that occasionally punches above its weight class.

So here’s the big question: is the Kingrinder P2 the breakout budget grinder we’ve all been waiting for, or is it just another overhyped compromise wrapped in plastic? Let’s dig in.

How We Got the P2 Grinder

We bought all three Kingrinders in the P range to test on CoffeeGeek

How We Tested the P2 Grinder

We bought all three grinders in the P range from Kingrinder and passed them around to several CoffeeGeek writers for testing and evaluation. The grinder was used extensively head to head with the 1Zpresso Q-Air, and also against the P1 model with its different burrset. We used it for almost every major brew method, including espresso and Chemex.

Out of the BoxP2 Grinder

Unboxing the Kingrinder P2 feels almost ironic. You get a plain cardboard box with zero design ambition. Inside? A bundle of surprisingly competent parts: the grinder body, the screw-on plastic grounds catch, a short cylindrical handle with a wooden knob, a rubber grip band, and a token cleaning brush. Hey, I guess the cleaning brush is good; after all, the more expensive 1Zpresso Q-Air doesn’t come with one.
The box is pretty basic.
The box opened shows some basic instructions and a lot of polystyrene.
Removing the top polystyrene cover shows the grinder, its handle and some other bits.
All the components of the grinder: handle, catch cup, main burr assembly top unit, silicone sleeve, and a cleaning brush

Unfortunately, Kingrinder still leans on polystyrene inserts to keep everything in place. It does the job, sure, but it’s the kind of packaging that makes me wince. Specialty coffee brands really need to move past polystyrene: it’s wasteful and hard to recycle. A snug cardboard cradle would protect this grinder just as well without leaving the planet holding the bill.

At just 330 grams (and 35g lighter than the Q-Air), the P2 feels closer to a travel thermos than a grinder. The body is made of ABS plastic, which may scream budget at first touch, but the assembly is tighter than expected. Nothing wobbles. There’s no sharp edges or weird mis-fits, hanging chads, the kind of thing you’d expect from a $45 product.

The handle is simple, all metal with a press-fit wooden knob. Threads on the catch cup are plastic on plastic, so you’ll want to be gentle to avoid cross-threading, but they’re surprisingly clean. Height clocks in at 14 cm, with a 5 cm diameter. Overall very compact and highly packable.
The body is all plastic, though the internal mounts for the burr and crank arm are metal.
The handle is quite nice considering the price point, and the cap fits snugly.
The brush that's included with the grinder.
The catch cup is all plastic and threaded, and unfortunately attracts static.
The upper chamber houses the spindle, burr assembly and grind adjustment components.
All the components of the grinder: handle, catch cup, main burr assembly top unit, silicone sleeve, and a cleaning brush

Where the value really starts to show is inside. The P2’s seven-burr stainless steel core is clearly the star of the show. And the burr mount system – all metal – also stands out with some really impressive stability. This This comes from a double bearing system on the internal driveshaft, something you wouldn’t expect to see in the build quality at this price point. Grinding a test 15g dose at a pourover setting reveals relatively smooth action and a nicely tactile resistance; it is not buttery smooth, but not grindhouse gritty either. 

Things change a bit when grinding for espresso: the action is a lot more gritty and chunky, and can require some effort.
Looking down inside the grinder shows the conical burrs and metal assembly.
The P2's grind selection dial is located under the upper compartment, and requires the catch bin to be removed before adjusting.
The two grinders, side by side. The Q Air is usually $20 more.
The Kingrinder has a slightly larger diameter than the 1ZPresso Q Air.

But then comes the mess: static.

The plastic catch cup becomes a clingy nightmare after your first grind. Fine particles cling to every inner surface like your grinder just ran through a hairdryer in a flour storm. And it doesn’t get better over time unless you introduce the Ross Droplet Technique (RDT). A spritz of water before grinding turns an annoying problem into a manageable one. Without it? You’ll be brushing coffee dust out of your keyboard. Blame the mix of materials.

Photo of static issues.
The P2 is a static monster at times, though a quick RDT spritz should resolve most static issues.
Static buildup inside the catch cup is pretty extreme too, and grinds fly everywhere when you're pouring them out. RDT should fix this.

The first impression overall is one of contrasts. The Kingrinder P2 feels toy-like, but performs with surprising precision. It’s dead simple to use, but messier than a toddler with glitter. Action is smooth for pour over grinds, chunky gritty as you get into espresso range. And yet, you get the sense Kingrinder knew exactly what corners they were cutting and which ones they absolutely did not.

Using theP2 Grinder

Using the Kingrinder P2 feels pretty straightforward. Load your beans, attache the handle, turn the bottom-mounted adjustment dial to your chosen grind, attach the grinds hopper, and start cranking. If you’ve used manual grinders before, this will feel familiar.

Now, about that adjustment dial math. Kingrinder says each click moves the burrs by 33 microns (µm), but we quickly realized that’s axial travel, the up and down movement, not the actual grind size change. After an iterative process of testing and recalibration based on real-world brewing results, our final model shows the grinder offers a surprisingly fine and consistent resolution of approximately 15 µm per click across its effective range.

After getting hands on with the P2 and dialing it in through real use, as well as limited particle size analysis (something we normally wouldn’t do for a product in this price range), here is our final revised grind guide based on clicks from zero, aligned with CoffeeGeek standards:

  • Espresso: 17 to 20 clicks (300 to 350 µm)

  • Moka Pot: 20 to 23 clicks (350 to 400 µm)

  • AeroPress, Fine to Regular: 27 to 37 clicks (450 to 600 µm)

  • V60 / Kalita Wave: 38 to 43 clicks (625 to 700 µm)

  • Chemex: 50 to 57 clicks (800 to 900 µm)

  • Press Pot (French Press): 70 to 77 clicks (1100 to 1200 µm)

Heads up. Once the P2 breaks in and gets seasoned, those numbers tend to drop by a click or two. These ranges reflect a grinder that’s had some miles on it.

Capacity is another highlight. The P2 swallows nearly 25 grams of beans (I measured 24.4 g max), which gives it a nice leg up on something like the 1Zpresso Q-Air, which tops out around 19.5 g. That extra volume makes the P2 more versatile if you like brewing larger mugs or sharing a pour-over with a friend.

One small disappointment for travellers: despite its compact size, the P2 does not fit inside an AeroPress plunger, which makes it a little less pack-friendly than you might hope.

But let’s not sugarcoat it. There are two pain points you can’t ignore.

First, the adjustment range. Despite a calculated resolution of about 15µm per click, dialing in espresso remains frustrating. The problem appears to be less about the step size itself and more about grind consistency. Each click finer seems to generate more fine coffee dust, which can choke an espresso machine. This effect turns a small adjustment into a dramatic jump from a gushing shot to a choked one. If espresso is your focus, you will likely need to adjust your dose to find the sweet spot between clicks.

We were not really able to get to the core of why this was happening. After all, 15µm is a decently tight range. My senior editor speculated it could be burr wobble brought on by flex in the ABS outer housing, which affects the grind more at the finer end. Because the cranking action is more “severe” at this finer grind, this could very well be the cause and effect, but I’ll have to leave the true discovery as to why to others. All I can say is, I experienced some frustrations dialing in this grinder for espresso.

Second, static. The plastic catch cup is clingier than my cat during a thunderstorm. Unless you spritz your beans with a bit of water (the Ross Droplet Technique), you’ll end up with grounds plastered everywhere: the cup walls, your counter, maybe even your laptop. A quick spray fixes it, but it’s one extra step you won’t forget.

Despite its quirks, the P2 produces cups with notable flavor separation for its price. However, it also generates a fair amount of fine particles in the pour-over range. To be clear, it’s still a relatively decent control over the fines production, especially at this price point. Compared to my old Hario Skerton and Mini, the fines out of this grinder are way, way more limited, but they are there. In dozens of pour over brews, I’ve seen a muddy coffee bed and an over-all slower drain time, which can mute some of the potential clarity.

Compared to the Timemore C2, the P2’s flavors can present themselves brighter and with a decent clarity, but we’re not talking 1Zpresso J series level output.

Ed.Note: Natia doesn’t have access to a Espro Bloom brewer, which is a new addition to our grinder test regimen. Because of this, I tested the P2 with the Bloom in the CoffeeGeek Lab, and it struggled to hit our 4:00-5:00 brew time in back to back tests once the grind was dialed in; this has to do with how many fines the grinder produces. Eventually, we hit our target brew time, but with a coarser grind, which resulted in a lower extraction ratio. Soon on CoffeeGeek, we’ll have a full feature on this brewer and why we use it to test grinders. In the case of the Kingrinder P2, it gets a C- rating.

P2 GrinderWho it's For

Kingrinder says the P2 is for espresso lovers, but honestly, that’s misleading. Perhaps they’re leaning on the more premium burr, while forgetting they have their ultra-budget adjustment system paired with it and possible flex from the ABS housing (that’s only speculation). It can grind fine enough, sure, but the nature of its adjustment steps makes it a poor match for anyone trying to fine-tune shots consistently.

Instead, the P2 shines for a different crowd: the pour-over devotee, the AeroPress lover, the bright-coffee enthusiast, the student who wants to ditch the blade grinder without blowing their UberEats budget. If you mostly brew with Hario V60, Kalita, AeroPress, or a French press, the P2 is a slam dunk for flavor per dollar. If you love lighter roasts and origin-driven profiles, even better.

Its portability makes it a strong contender for travellers and campers too, though again, it’s worth flagging that it doesn’t fit inside an AeroPress chamber, a definite perk of the competing 1Zpresso Q-Air. Still, it’s small, lightweight, and requires no tools to maintain.

So no, it’s not for espresso nerds. But for just about everyone else taking their first steps into better coffee, the P2 is an incredibly rewarding upgrade.

P2 GrinderComparisons

1Zpresso Q-Air

At roughly a third more in cost, the 1Zpresso Q-Air offers a better build, slightly improved shaft stability (though the P2’s own double-bearing setup holds its own surprisingly well), and more viable espresso potential. Also of note: the Q-Air’s spindle can be driven by a cordless screwdriver or drill (a selling point 1ZPresso pushes often) but the P2’s spindle, while robust, is a square mount style, and not the hexagonal style of the Q-Air. Because of this, you can’t drive the spindle with a cordless screwdriver unless you buy a special bit attachment.

On initial inspection the burrs seem very similar in design, but looking closer, you see the 1Zpresso burrs are more refined. In the cup, the Q-Air obviously has the better burrset, producing less fines in the brew coffee ranges. Cup clarity is a bit better too.

As we noted in our CoffeeGeek review of the 1Zpresso Q-Air, what you’re really paying for is consistency, smoother action, powered-by-drill options, and better ergonomics. Also, it fits inside an AeroPress. That matters for travel folks.
Two grinders, side by side.
The Kingrinder has a slightly larger diameter than the 1ZPresso Q Air.
The Q-Air and P2, looking down inside.
The Kingrinder P2 does not fit inside an Aeropress, though its main competitor, the Q-Air from 1Zpresso, does.

Timemore C2 Grinder

Often neck‑and‑neck with the P2 in budget grinder conversations on reddit, which is a bit weird since it almost double the cost. The Timemore C2 has an all metal body and slightly smoother grind action, but delivers a heavier‑bodied, more chocolate‑forward cup. Great for espresso in the C2 ESP variant, but in flavor clarity for pour‑over? While the P2 seemed to produce a bit more fines, it also brings an additional level of nuance to the cup that the C2 seems to lack. I’d put it down the much more modern burr design in the P2.

OXO Brew Conical Burr (electric)

If you want the convenience of an electric grinder under $100, the OXO Brew is hard to beat. But it’s big, noisy, and not as precise in grind distribution as the P2. Flavor‑wise, you get more boulders and more fines which will deliver a muddier cup.

At least that’s what my editor says: I don’t have an OXO Brew to test, but he does, and he’s tested it, including against the P2 and Q-Air.

Suffice to say, for clarity and travel, manual still wins. For convenience, the OXO’s not bad. It’s just not very good either.

P2 GrinderWhat's the Value Like

The P2 is a value outlier, and I don’t say that lightly. For about $45, you get a burr set capable of producing pour-over cups that could honestly fool you into thinking they came from a $150 grinder. It’s not just passable. It’s impressive.

But that value comes bundled with trade-offs. The plastic housing keeps the cost low, but adds static and raises long-term durability questions. The adjustment steps limit espresso versatility. And the entire experience, from packaging to workflow, reminds you that corners were cut.

Still, for someone starting out, or upgrading from a blade grinder, this is a $45 mini masterclass in flavor clarity. The grinder doesn’t try to do everything at a five star level, but it does attempt to give you an upgraded economy seat experience given it’s price tier, and I feel it’s done that.

ConclusionP2 Grinder

The Kingrinder P2 is a budget grinder full of contradictions. On one hand, it delivers good enough filter coffee clarity that can compare with grinders three times its price. On the other hand, it’s wrapped in plastic, generates static like a balloon at a kid’s party, produces 2018-era fines, and struggles with espresso consistency.

For pour‑over fans chasing bright, fruit‑forward hints of clarity (while not minding the slight muddiness in the filter bed), the P2 is an easy recommendation. It’s light, portable, and remarkably capable once you learn to tame the static with a spritz of water. The burrs are the real story here: capable of producing a cup that rivals much more expensive gear.

That said, the compromises are real. The quirky adjustments make dialing in espresso more luck than science, and long‑term durability is still an open question. If you want a smoother grind, sturdier build, less fines and better ergonomics, the 1Zpresso Q‑Air is a strong alternative, though you’ll pay about a third more for the privilege.

In the end, the P2 isn’t trying to be a premium all‑rounder. It’s a filter‑focused disruptor with an espresso side hustle that proves you don’t need to spend $150+ to enjoy bright, specialty-level flavor profiles. If you’re on a very tight budget or need a travel‑friendly option, the P2 earns its place in your kit, with a few caveats you’ll want to accept going in.
